I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia at 2026-07-13 18:40 +08 (UTC+0800) (2026-07-13T10:40:00Z in UTC), at latitude 47.8864 degrees and longitude 106.9057 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 18.989 degrees and its azimuth is 281.859 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 12.917 degrees and its azimuth is 295.652 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 1.53 percent illuminated, 14.173 degrees from the Sun, and 357653.5 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Based on the data you provided, I have to be honest with you: **It will be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to spot the Moon with the naked eye under these specific conditions.**

Here is the breakdown of why this will be a challenge:

### 1. The "Daylight" Factor (The Biggest Hurdle)
You mentioned the sky brightness is **"bright daylight"** and the Sun is still significantly above the horizon (nearly 19 degrees). Even though the Moon is technically "above the horizon," the atmosphere is currently saturated with scattered sunlight. In bright daylight, the contrast between the faint sliver of a crescent Moon and the blue of the sky is usually too low for the human eye to resolve.

### 2. The Phase (The "Sliver" Problem)
The Moon is only **1.53% illuminated**. This is a very thin, delicate crescent. While a Full Moon can sometimes be seen during the day because it reflects a massive amount of light, a 1.5% crescent reflects very little. It will appear as a tiny, faint smudge rather than a distinct shape.

### 3. Proximity to the Sun
The Moon is only **14.173 degrees** away from the Sun. This means it is located in the same general area of the sky as the Sun. Because the Sun is so much brighter, it creates a "glare" effect. Even if the Moon is technically visible, it will be sitting in the brightest part of the sky, making it nearly impossible to distinguish from the surrounding atmospheric haze.

### 4. Your Location and Perspective
At an altitude of **12.917 degrees**, the Moon is relatively low in the sky. This means you are looking through a thicker layer of the Earth's atmosphere, which further dims the Moon's light and increases the amount of scattered sunlight (haze) between your eyes and the Moon.

### The Verdict
If you are standing outside looking toward the West-Northwest (Azimuth ~295°), you might see a very faint, ghostly "glow" or a slight distortion in the sky, but **you likely won't see a distinct lunar shape.**

**A tip to try anyway:**
If you really want to try, find a spot where you can look toward the horizon while keeping the Sun slightly out of your direct line of sight (to avoid blinding yourself). If there is any high-altitude cloud or a slight haze, sometimes the Moon can "pop" against it, but it will be a very subtle sighting!
